To immure someone means to shut them inside an enclosed space — like a prison, a room, or walls — so that they cannot get out. It conveys a powerful sense of total confinement, isolation, and the removal of freedom.

Think of it this way: if you build a wall around someone, or lock them inside walls with no way out, you have immured them.

1. The Literal Meaning — Physical Confinement

In its most direct sense, to immure someone is to physically enclose them within walls, trapping them inside a place from which escape is impossible or extremely difficult. Historically, this could mean:

  • Locking a person inside a dungeon or a cell with thick stone walls around them.
  • In its darkest historical use, it even referred to sealing a person inside a wall — literally entombing someone alive within the structure of a building. This was a rare but real form of punishment or execution in ancient times.

So the word carries a very visual, architectural weight. The walls are not just background — they are the instrument of the confinement.

2. The Figurative Meaning — General Imprisonment or Isolation

More broadly, and more commonly in modern usage, immure means to imprison, confine, or shut away — even when physical walls aren't the central image. It describes a condition of being completely cut off from the outside world, whether by force or by circumstance.

For example, you might say someone is immured in a remote location, or even immured in a situation they cannot escape — like a trapped routine or a self-imposed isolation.

These examples show you the word in action across different situations:

  • "The political prisoner was immured in a cold cell for years, with no contact with the outside world."

→ He was physically locked away behind walls.

  • "The monks chose to immure themselves in the monastery, dedicating their lives entirely to prayer and silence."

→ Here, the people willingly cut themselves off from the world. This is important — you can immure yourself, not just be immured by someone else.

  • "She felt immured by grief, unable to step outside or reconnect with the people around her."

→ A figurative use. No physical walls exist, but the feeling of being trapped and shut in is the same.

  • "The dictator immured his opponents in remote prisons, ensuring they would never be heard from again."

→ Classic use: an authority figure forcibly confines someone.
Who Does the Immuring? Active vs. Passive Use

This is an important nuance.

  • Someone can immure another person — an authority, a captor, a government.

"The king immured his brother in the tower."

  • Someone can be immured (passive) — they are the victim of the confinement.

"She was immured for decades without trial."

  • Someone can immure themselves (reflexive) — they voluntarily withdraw and shut themselves away from the world. This is a common and meaningful use of the word.

"After his loss, he immured himself in his apartment and refused to see anyone."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Words like imprison, confine, incarcerate, and lock up are related, but immure is distinct in a few ways:

  • It emphasizes walls and total enclosure more than any other synonym. The image of being surrounded by walls — shut completely inside — is central to the word.
  • It carries a stronger sense of isolation and permanence. To immure someone suggests they are cut off not just from freedom, but from the entire outside world.
  • It has a literary, formal tone. You would rarely hear it in casual conversation. It appears most often in literary writing, historical accounts, journalism, and formal speech. Choosing this word signals seriousness and gravity.
  • It can be used figuratively with great force. Because the word carries such a strong visual and emotional weight, writers use it to describe emotional, psychological, or social confinement — not just physical imprisonment.

Immure is not a neutral word. It carries a heavy, somber emotional quality. When you read or hear it, it evokes:

  • Darkness and enclosure
  • The removal of freedom and human connection
  • A sense of being forgotten or cut off from the world
  • Sometimes: suffering, punishment, or tragic self-withdrawal

It is a word that feels like what it means — heavy, enclosed, final.

What it meansTo shut someone inside walls; to imprison or confine completely
Who it applies toA person (or group) — never objects
DirectionCan be done to someone, or done by someone to themselves
ToneFormal, literary, serious
Key imageWalls surrounding a person with no way out

In one sentence: To immure someone is to trap them completely inside a confined space — physically, socially, or emotionally — cutting them off entirely from the outside world.
